bibliography.abstract: Human mobility data are fundamental to Web-based location services and broader urban applications, and mobility generation provides synthetic trajectories when real data are costly or inaccessible. Although recent mobility generators have incorporated collective mobility patterns, they primarily focus on individual trajectories and aggregate population dynamics, leaving evolving community structures formed by user-location interactions insufficiently modeled. In this paper, we study community-consistent human mobility generation. To this end, we formulate mobility generation as the generation of dynamic user-location graphs to model community structures and propose MOTION, a Multi-agent framework for cOmmuniTy-consIstent human mObility geNeration. MOTION consists of user agents, location agents, and a global manager agent. MOTION first detects coherent communities from historical mobility using the Leiden algorithm and extracts community-conditioned interaction priors to guide the generation process. Guided by these priors, the user agents plan mobility, search destination candidates, and infer user movements from the individual view. In parallel, selectively activated location agents infer likely user arrivals from the community view. The manager coordinates both views, diagnoses interactions causing deviations, and attributes targeted reflection signals to revise user decisions, location attraction, and source-user selection. Experiments on two real-world datasets show that MOTION outperforms baselines by at least 4.05% across reported metrics of individual trajectories, population and flow distributions, and community and graph structures. Further analyses confirm its robustness, privacy preservation, and downstream utility. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MOTION-04C4.
bibliography.title: Beyond Trajectory Statistics: Community-Consistent Human Mobility Generation via Evolving User-Location Graphs

en.what: The authors developed MOTION, a multi-agent framework that generates synthetic human mobility by modeling dynamic user-location graphs and preserving community structures. The model uses the Leiden algorithm to extract historical interaction priors, which guide interacting user, location, and manager agents to refine trajectory decisions from both individual and community perspectives. Evaluated on two real-world datasets, MOTION outperformed existing mobility generation baselines by at least 4.05% across metrics measuring individual trajectories, spatial flow distributions, and graph structures.
en.why: By moving beyond individual trajectory statistics to capture evolving community-level interaction patterns, this approach produces synthetic mobility data that better reflects complex social and urban graph topologies for downstream spatial computing applications.
